_comment: Central balance sheet for the campaign system. This file is the single
source of truth: PHP reads it directly for multiplayer, and
tools/build-campaign-config.mjs generates js/data/actions.js from it for
solo play. Change a number here and both sides change together.
All money is in rupees. Support effects are percentage points.
Outcome weights are relative and need not sum to 100.
The actions below are fictional game mechanics. The 'risky' ones abstract
questionable political behaviour into a cost, a dice roll and a
consequence - they describe no real-world method and never explain how
anything would be done.

heat._consequenceComment: Chance of a consequence firing after an action = heat/100 * chanceFactor, floored below minHeat.
heat._coolComment: Heat cools slightly at each round end. Without it heat only ever climbs, so a single risky round would mark a player for the rest of the campaign and the risk system becomes a one-way door rather than a dial.

_comment: The sitting MLA's party starts ahead in their own seat. How far ahead is
rolled per seat from the game seed, so the map is not uniform and players
cannot assume every incumbent is equally hard to shift.
These numbers are a balance between two requirements that pull against each
other. Incumbency has to be a real advantage, or the verified MLA data is
decoration; but the real result must not simply replay, or the game is over
before anyone campaigns. partySwingSpread is what buys the second: each game
rolls one swing per party across every seat, so some open with a dominant
incumbent bloc and others with a genuine four-way fight.
As tuned (measure with: npm run measure:board, 60 games):
incumbents hold their own seat in 74 of 117 on average, range 22-110
the largest bloc opens on 76 on average, range 44-113
the incumbent party leads the board in roughly two games in three
After four players campaign, about a quarter of elections end hung.
othersHandicap keeps the unplayable Others bucket where it belongs: it holds
a couple of real seats and can win a handful, but it never gets a statewide
swing and never sweeps.
Advantage, swing and spread are all in percentage points of support.
Election day. Each seat is decided on the shares in it plus a little
noise, so a narrow lead is not a guarantee and a close race can go
either way. seatNoise is in percentage points.
undecidedWeight is what stops the board being won by turning up.
A seat holds raw campaign influence, and the shares are worked out
from it - so one rally in an untouched seat reads as 100% of nothing
much. Without a counterweight the best play would be a single cheap
move in all 117, and choosing where to campaign would stop mattering
entirely.
So part of every seat stays undecided, and that part is larger the
less work has been done there: undecided = k / (k + influence). At
k=14 a seat with one rally in it is about three quarters a coin toss;
a seat somebody has really campaigned in is barely a toss at all. The
undecided part splits at random on the day, which is what makes
breadth a gamble and depth a decision.
When a seat stops being led and starts being won.
Leading is where a seat stands today and can be taken back tomorrow.
Winning it is final: nobody can campaign there again, including the
winner, and it counts toward a district being permanently controlled.
Two conditions, and both matter. share says nobody else is close;
influence says the seat has actually been campaigned in rather than being
one a party wandered into while the others were elsewhere. Without the
second, one opening investment in an empty seat would lock it forever.
At 25 influence a seat costs about ten crore to lock if nobody contests
it — two rounds of allowance spent in one place. That is deliberate: it
leaves a rival a round to notice and come in, which is what makes the
conflict rule matter, and it keeps the permanent layer to roughly ten
seats a campaign rather than the whole board.
Post-election government formation. Version 1 allows two human players in
a coalition; the structure allows more later.
A proposal must be accepted by the other player, and either side can walk
away, in which case the talks fail and another pairing can be tried.

resourceTerms.label: Split campaign resources equally next time
Proposer gets first call on resources
Partner gets first call on resources

_comment: A fictional oversight mechanic layered on Political Heat.
Players may report a rival once each. Reports do not equal guilt: the
outcome is rolled against a hidden evidence score, so an innocent player
can be cleared even with three reports, and ganging up does not reliably
remove anyone.
Evidence is never shown to players. Weights are shifted by evidenceBias:
positive means more likely when evidence is high, negative means less.

evidence._comment: All contributions are capped so no single factor decides it.

outcomes.label: CLEARED
outcomes.text: The inquiry found nothing to answer. Your campaign carries on.

outcomes.label: WARNING
outcomes.text: A formal warning is recorded against your campaign.

outcomes.label: FINE
outcomes.text: Your campaign is fined.

outcomes.label: MAJOR FINE
outcomes.text: A substantial fine is imposed after a damaging finding.

outcomes.label: CAMPAIGN RESTRICTION

outcomes.label: DISQUALIFICATION
outcomes.text: Your candidature is cancelled under the rules of the game.

insufficientFunds._comment: If a fine cannot be paid, the budget is emptied and the rest is taken out in other ways. A budget must never go negative.
insufficientFunds.text: Your campaign could not pay the fine in full, and paid for it in other ways.

opened.text: Investigation announced — public support falls slightly.

_comment: Twenty rounds. One to fifteen are the campaign; fifteen is the checkpoint
where the weakest campaign can be eliminated; sixteen to twenty are the
run to government.
The host picks the round length from durationOptions before the game
starts. Two minutes is the default and the floor — below that nobody can
read a board, let alone decide anything.
There is no cap on moves per round. What limits a round is the money a
player has and the moment they press END ROUND.
Two rounds get a longer break: the one where alliances close and the one
where the review runs. Both put something on the screen that has to be
read and decided on rather than glanced at, and nine seconds is a glance.
Cash and debt are tracked separately and cash may never go negative.
Loans are the interesting decision: money now against a bill four rounds
later, at a rate that hurts. Borrowing after round 16 is refused because
the bill would land after the campaign has closed, which would make late
borrowing free.
The bank lends against capacity rather than appetite, and a payment that
cannot be met carries forward with a penalty rather than clearing. The
default block below is what remains of the old rule and now applies only
where a campaign is beyond recovery.
Twenty per cent, due four rounds later.
A loan is lent against capacity, not appetite: cash in hand, the round
allowances certain to arrive before it falls due, and the grants already
being paid by districts already held — less what is already owed. Nothing
speculative counts, so nobody can borrow against seats they might win.
A payment that cannot be met is not a default and does not clear the
debt. What the campaign has goes toward it, the balance carries into the
next round, and missedPenaltyRate is added to whatever is left. It keeps
carrying and keeps taking the penalty until it is cleared.

default.text: You could not repay. Word of the default is all over the campaign.

_comment: Two ways to raise money mid-campaign, with opposite characters.
A grant application is honest and unreliable: it costs a real amount of
work, usually returns less than it cost on its own, and carries no heat.
It is worth doing because the development spending also moves support.
Underground funding is the mirror image: it can pay several times over, but
it is the fastest way to raise heat in the game and can be taken away again
by an investigation. Both are fictional game mechanics; neither describes
any real-world method.

grant.label: Apply for a Grant
grant.blurb: Fund visible development work and apply for matching support.

outcomes.label: Application approved in full
outcomes.text: The work is done and the grant came through in full.

outcomes.label: Partly funded
outcomes.text: Some of the money came back, and the work is visible.

outcomes.label: A token amount
outcomes.text: Barely worth the paperwork, but the work still counts.

outcomes.label: Application refused
outcomes.text: No funding at all. At least the development was noticed.

round would drown out the decisions players actually made.
Events land on a named constituency or across the campaign, never as a
silent adjustment.

_reachComment: Why dearer actions reach further rather than simply hitting harder.
Every seat is normalised to 100 across five parties, so a large gain in
one seat is compressed on the way in: +4 raw lands as roughly +3, while
+2 raw lands as roughly +1.9. Raw support therefore has sharply
diminishing returns, and an action costing two and a half times as much
bought barely a tenth more effect. With three moves a round, that made
money almost irrelevant — the opposite of the intended balance, and
measurably worse than not spending at all once interest was counted.
Reach fixes it in the direction the subject suggests anyway. A doorstep
campaign moves one constituency. Media coverage and a statewide push are
seen in several. The extra seats take a fraction of the effect, so
spending more genuinely buys more — but it buys breadth, not certainty,
and choosing the right seat to aim at still matters more than the size of
the cheque. Bad outcomes spread the same way: a media campaign that goes

_comment: Thresholds for the round-results screen. All display, no rules.
closeRaceSeats decides when the top two are worth calling a close race.
Set it too high and every round looks like a photo finish, which stops
meaning anything; too low and genuinely tight elections pass unremarked.
maxSeatChangesShown caps the list of constituencies that changed hands.
Early rounds can flip forty seats at once, and a wall of them is worse
than a count — the rest are summarised as a total.
Opponents for the parties nobody is playing, so the scoreboard always has
four competitors and a solo game is still an election.
The AI plays by exactly the same rules as a human: the same actions, the
same costs, the same weighted outcomes, the same heat, the same money,
the same consequences when it runs hot. Its round is bounded by what it
can afford, exactly as a human round is. It has no extra information and
no extra money. What differs between the profiles is temperament: how
much risk it will take, how tightly it targets, and how much it plays
for districts rather than for the next seat.
Names are drawn at random per game from the pools below. They are ordinary
Punjabi given names and surnames combined freely; any resemblance to a
particular living politician would be coincidence, and none of the pools
is built from real officeholders.

profiles.label: Steady
profiles.blurb: Works the marginals and builds a district at a time.

profiles.label: Ambitious
profiles.blurb: Spends hard and takes the occasional gamble.

profiles.label: Reckless
profiles.blurb: Runs hot and hopes the scrutiny lands elsewhere.

_partyNameComment: Party names are built from three pools: where it says it speaks for,
what it says it is for, and what kind of body it calls itself. That is
the shape most new parties' names actually take, so four of them sound
like they belong to the same election without any two being alike.
Every combination is invented. The pools are chosen so that no pairing
of them lands on the name of a real party, and an opponent never takes
a name, colour, symbol or abbreviation a player has already used.
slogans: A fair deal for every village

_menuComment: Which menu each action appears under.
There are three actions in the game. Campaigning is money into an area
and is the only one anybody needs; the negative campaign and the
corruption/bribe are optional modifiers a player may attach to it.
This lives in the config rather than the interface so adding an action
puts it in the right place without anyone editing a screen.

_comment: How much a single move may cost. The floor keeps a move meaningful; the
ceiling is a multiple of the action's own cost, so a rally is still a
rally however rich the campaign.
None of this caps a round. A player with twenty crore saved may spend all
of it in one round across as many seats as they like.
_curveComment: How an amount converts to effect: scale = (amount / baseCost) ^ curve.
At 0.5 this is a square root, and spreading one sum across N seats is
worth sqrt(N) times aiming it at one — a very strong pull toward breadth.
Raising the exponent toward 1 flattens that: at c, spreading is worth
N^(1-c). This is the single lever that decides whether the game rewards
reading the map or simply touching every seat.
_entryComment: The most a campaign may put behind its first move into a seat.
Getting in is cheap and capped. Anybody may walk into an open seat for a
crore, so nobody can buy their way in ahead of everybody else — an
opening is a foot in the door, not a purchase. Once a campaign has a
presence there the cap is gone.
It is also what makes the opening conflict possible: five campaigns
entering one seat all commit the same crore, all match, and all bounce

_comment: Corruption and bribery, as one optional modifier on a campaign.
There used to be a menu of them. There is one now, because choosing
between four ways to cheat was a decision about vocabulary rather
than about strategy: what a player is actually deciding is whether
to take the risk at all.
It is a fictional mechanic and nothing more: a cost, a weighted
table, a lot of heat, and a real chance of an investigation. It
describes no method and explains how nothing would be done. The
interesting part is what happens when it goes wrong, which it does
three times in ten.
Nothing in the game requires it. A campaign funded and fought
entirely on ordinary money can win, and does in the balance runs.
Player profiles, levels, achievements and the leaderboard score.
Everything here is counted from games the server actually ran. A solo
game runs entirely in the browser, so its result is self-reported: it is
recorded on the player's own profile and shown to them, but it never
feeds the global leaderboard, because there is no way to tell a real solo
win from a crafted request. Verified games are the ones that count for
rank.
The score formula is configurable on purpose. It weights winning and
seats rather than turning up, so grinding games is not a strategy.

level._comment: Level is score-based, on a widening curve so early levels come quickly.

_startingBudgetComment: Nobody starts with money any more. A campaign is funded round by round:
income.perRound arrives at the start of every round and whatever is not
spent stays. Over twenty rounds that is a hundred crore a player, and a
four-player election generates four hundred — but only ever five crore at
a time, so saving for a big move is a real decision rather than a footnote.

_comment: The round allowance. This is income, not a spending cap: a player who
has saved may spend everything they hold in one round.
Credited exactly once per round per player, keyed by round number, so a
refresh or a reconnection cannot pay somebody twice.
Districts and the three regions of Punjab.
Holding every seat in a district pays its grant every round for as long
as the hold lasts, and the money is locked to the region the district
sits in. That is what makes the map worth reading: a fourteen-seat
district in Malwa pays for a Malwa campaign and nothing else.
The grant scales with district size between the floor and the ceiling.
tools/build-regions.mjs does the scaling and writes js/data/regions.js;
the district-to-region mapping lives there because it is geography, not
balance.
How many districts a player may name as priority targets. Priority
is a statement of intent, not ownership — rivals can and do campaign
in the same places.
The ceiling is the number of districts Punjab actually has. The
brief asked for up to seventy; Punjab has twenty-three, and
inventing another forty-seven was not an option.
Two players may agree to fight the election together. Offers close at
the end of the deadline round; after that an alliance is locked until
the result, so nobody can shop for a better partner at round nineteen.
Allies see each other's priority districts. They do not see each
other's cash, their heat, or anything they did quietly.
At the end of the checkpoint round the weakest campaign may be put out
of the election — but only if it is genuinely out of it. A player still
within reach of the majority survives, because a comeback is the best
thing that can happen in a game like this.
Never applied when two or fewer players remain.
